chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by the Kephalaia dialogue apparatus plus institutional/pastoral differentiation between “sinners” and “catechumens,” framed as moral-educative punishment (children vs servants). It does not preserve a clearly separable cosmos→cosmos correspondential substrate; even the scattered cosmological phrases (“throne in the light,” “great fire”) occur inside an applied, disciplinary comparison aimed at community categories.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Hagiographic/dialogue frame: catechumen questions the “apostle,” “my master,” references to lessons “written…in the books.” The content is posed as community catechesis (sinners vs catechumens), not impersonal cosmological exposition.
Bridging narration/attribution (“Then the lord speaks…”) introducing the topic as two ‘lessons.’ This is editorial scaffolding rather than substrate teaching.

Direct address and announcement of instruction (“Now, listen… I will recount… proclaim to you”) focused on catechumens’ ‘education’ during transmigration—application to an audience category (institutional layer).

Extended moral analogy contrasting discipline of children vs servants (rebuke, striking, chains, prison). This is ethical/social illustration aimed at community formation, not a systematic cosmic-degree mapping.

Although it contains scattered cosmological vocabulary (“throne in the light,” “great fire”), the paragraph’s structure remains an applied comparison about catechumens’ vs sinners’ treatment and fate. No stable, extractable cosmos→cosmos correspondential sequence is recoverable from the lacunose text.
Concluding benediction/valuation of catechumens (“Blessed are you… chosen and ordained…”) with condemnation of others’ ‘end.’ This is paraenetic and institutional rather than substrate cosmology.
